course_information.title: Retail Pricing Fundamentals
course_information.description: Understand retail price, cost, gross profit, margin, markup, promotions, and responsible price communication.
course_information.scope: General independent hardware retail; store-specific rules are not supplied
course_information.restrictions: No legal, tax, HR, accounting, or licensed-professional advice. Follow store procedures and refer restricted decisions.
learning_objectives: Distinguish retail price, item cost, gross profit, margin, and markup.
Calculate a basic gross margin and explain how it differs from markup.
Recognize how discounts and fees affect gross profit.
Use approved procedures to investigate price differences.
Explain prices and promotions clearly without making unauthorized changes.

lessons.title: Understand Price, Cost, and Gross Profit
lessons.objective: Identify the main numbers behind a retail sale.
lessons.why_this_matters: A selling price does not tell you how much a store earns.

content_sections.heading: Start with the selling price
content_sections.text: Retail price is the amount charged to the customer before applicable taxes. Product cost is what the business pays for an item under its accounting method. The two amounts are not the same.

content_sections.heading: Calculate gross profit
content_sections.text: For a simple single-item example, gross profit dollars equal selling price minus item cost. A $20 item that costs $12 produces $8 of gross profit before other expenses.

content_sections.heading: Know what is missing
content_sections.text: Gross profit is not net profit. Rent, wages, payment fees, freight treatment, shrink, and other expenses affect the business. Stores may account for costs differently.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A manager sees a $20 shelf price and assumes the store earns $20. The item cost is $12, so the simple gross profit is $8, not $20.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s look at selling price and item cost before discussing profitability.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Confusing revenue with profit; assuming gross profit pays every expense.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask the owner or finance lead when item costs, freight allocations, or accounting definitions are unclear.

optional_practice.question: A $20 sale with a $12 item cost has how many dollars of gross profit?

lessons.title: Separate Margin from Markup
lessons.objective: Calculate margin and markup using the correct denominator.
lessons.why_this_matters: These percentages look similar but answer different questions.

content_sections.heading: Gross margin
content_sections.text: Gross margin percentage is gross profit divided by selling price, multiplied by 100. For a $20 sale and $12 cost, $8 ÷ $20 = 40%.

content_sections.heading: Markup
content_sections.text: Markup percentage is gross profit divided by cost, multiplied by 100. For the same item, $8 ÷ $12 is about 66.7%.

content_sections.heading: Avoid mix-ups
content_sections.text: A 40% margin is not a 40% markup. Verify which measure your POS or report uses before comparing numbers.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A department lead says the item has a 40% markup. You review the $20 price and $12 cost and explain that it has a 40% margin and about a 66.7% markup.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Margin divides by selling price; markup divides by cost.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Using cost as the margin denominator; comparing markup with margin reports.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate when reports use different cost definitions or include returns and discounts differently.

lessons.title: See How Discounts Change Profit
lessons.objective: Explain how a discount affects gross profit.
lessons.why_this_matters: A small price change can create a large change in gross profit.

content_sections.heading: Run the numbers
content_sections.text: If an item sells for $20 and costs $12, gross profit is $8. Discount the selling price to $16 and gross profit falls to $4, assuming cost stays the same.

content_sections.heading: Look beyond one item
content_sections.text: A promotion may increase unit sales or bring in related purchases. Those results are not guaranteed. Compare sales, gross profit, and the promotion goal.

content_sections.heading: Check the full offer
content_sections.text: Coupons, bundles, vendor support, and loyalty discounts may change the effective price or cost. Follow approved promotion rules and confirm the actual terms.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks for 20% off a $20 item. You calculate the new price as $16 and recognize that gross profit drops from $8 to $4 at the assumed $12 cost.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Before approving a discount, I need to check the promotion rules and its impact.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Treating 20% off as a 20% reduction in profit; promising unapproved discounts.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a manager or pricing owner before overriding prices or stacking offers.

lessons.title: Investigate Price Differences
lessons.objective: Respond to mismatched shelf and register prices.
lessons.why_this_matters: A mismatch can frustrate customers and undermine trust.

content_sections.heading: Check the evidence
content_sections.text: Confirm the product identifier, package size, shelf label, advertised offer, and register entry. Similar-looking items may have different prices.

content_sections.heading: Follow store policy
content_sections.text: Do not invent a price-match or adjustment policy. Escalate corrections and customer resolutions to the authorized person.

content_sections.heading: Fix the cause
content_sections.text: Once the immediate customer issue is addressed, report the mismatch so the shelf tag, system record, or promotion sign can be corrected.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer points to a $9.99 shelf label, but the register shows $12.99. Verify the SKU and promotion details, then follow the store’s price-discrepancy procedure.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Thank you for showing me. I’ll check the item and shelf label, then get the right person to resolve it.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Blaming the customer; changing a price without authority; leaving a wrong shelf tag in place.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate disputed promotions, tax issues, and overrides beyond your authorization.

optional_practice.question: What should you do first when a shelf price and register price disagree?

options.A: Assume the register is always right
options.B: Verify the item and signage, then follow store policy
options.C: Remove the shelf label without reporting it
options.D: Promise any price the customer wants

optional_practice.explanation: Verification and approved resolution protect the customer and store.

lessons.title: Explain Pricing Clearly and Fairly
lessons.why_this_matters: Clear pricing builds trust even when customers decide not to buy.

content_sections.heading: Describe the offer
content_sections.text: State the actual selling price, promotion conditions, quantity limits, and dates when applicable. Verify advertised details before making a claim.

content_sections.heading: Discuss value
content_sections.text: Compare useful differences such as pack quantity, durability, included accessories, and warranty terms when supported by the product information.

content_sections.heading: Stay within authority
content_sections.text: Do not promise competitor matching, future pricing, tax treatment, or special discounts without confirmation. Avoid claims that an item is “the best” without a clear basis.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer compares two packs of screws. One costs more but contains twice as many pieces. You compare the unit count and price per piece before recommending a choice.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s compare what is included and the cost per piece.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Using vague “better quality” claims; omitting offer conditions; making unauthorized promises.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Refer unusual price requests, complaints about advertising, and unclear warranty terms to management.

optional_practice.question: What is the best way to explain a two-pack price difference?

options.A: Focus only on the more expensive sticker
options.B: Compare quantity, features, and verified terms
